stem: A 61-year-old woman has a heart rate of 170/min with a regular narrow-complex rhythm 15 minutes after an abdominal operation. Her blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg and she is awake. The team chooses a beta-blocker infusion and wants its effect to wear off within minutes if her blood pressure falls.
oneliner: 61F + 15 min post abdominal surgery + HR 170 regular narrow-complex + BP 118/74 + beta-blocker infusion wanted with effect gone within minutes → which drug?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate drug?

whyNot.B: Hepatic metabolism, **half-life hours**; not an ultrashort infusion
whyNot.C: Non-selective with a **long half-life**; not ultrashort
whyNot.D: Class III drug with beta-blocking action; **long-acting** and prolongs QT

why: **Perioperative SVT where a minutes-long effect is wanted** = esmolol. It is a **cardioselective** beta-blocker broken down by **red-cell esterases**, so its half-life is about 9 minutes.

drug.name: Esmolol
drug.how: Rapid hydrolysis by red-cell esterases, half-life about 9 min
drug.use: Perioperative tachycardia and hypertension, SVT, aortic dissection

stem: A 38-year-old man has had two episodes of acute pancreatitis. His fasting triglycerides are 1,850 mg/dL, LDL cholesterol is low, and VLDL is elevated. His father and a brother have the same lipid problem. He does not drink alcohol, has no diabetes and normal thyroid tests. A drug is started to prevent further attacks.
oneliner: 38M + 2 episodes of pancreatitis + TG 1,850 + high VLDL + father and brother affected + no alcohol, diabetes or thyroid disease → which drug?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate drug?

whyNot.A: Lowers **LDL**; effect on triglycerides is modest
whyNot.C: Blocks intestinal cholesterol absorption; lowers **LDL**, little effect on triglycerides
whyNot.D: Fiber with a small cholesterol effect; **not strong enough**

why: **Very high TG and VLDL with pancreatitis** = familial hypertriglyceridemia. A **fibrate** activates PPAR-alpha, which raises lipoprotein lipase and lowers VLDL the most.

drug.name: Gemfibrozil
drug.how: PPAR-alpha agonist: more lipoprotein lipase, lower VLDL and triglycerides
drug.watch: Myopathy (esp. with statins), cholesterol gallstones, GI upset

stem: A 65-year-old man has had crushing chest pain for 1 hour. ECG shows 3 mm ST elevation in leads V2 to V5. His blood pressure is 134/82 mm Hg. He has no history of bleeding, recent surgery or stroke, and the nearest cardiac catheterization laboratory is 3 hours away. Aspirin has been given.
oneliner: 65M + crushing chest pain 1 h + 3 mm ST elevation V2-V5 + BP 134/82 + no bleeding history, surgery or stroke + cath lab 3 h away → which drug?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate additional treatment to limit infarct size?

whyNot.B: Lowers remodeling later but **does not reopen the artery**
whyNot.C: Adds inotropy and arrhythmia risk; **no effect on infarct size**
whyNot.D: Treats congestion; his **BP and lungs show no overload**

why: **STEMI within hours, no contraindication, and no timely PCI** = reperfusion with a fibrinolytic. **Alteplase (tPA)** converts plasminogen to plasmin, which lyses the coronary clot.

drug.name: Alteplase
drug.how: Converts plasminogen to plasmin, lysing fibrin
drug.use: STEMI (no PCI available), ischemic stroke within window, massive PE
drug.watch: Bleeding, intracranial hemorrhage; contraindicated with recent bleeding, surgery or stroke

stem: A 72-year-old man with atrial fibrillation not on anticoagulation has sudden weakness of the left face, arm and leg that began 90 minutes ago. Blood pressure is 156/90 mm Hg and blood glucose is 110 mg/dL. A noncontrast CT of the head shows no hemorrhage. He has no recent surgery, bleeding or head trauma.
oneliner: 72M + atrial fibrillation, no anticoagulant + sudden left face, arm, leg weakness 90 min ago + BP 156/90, glucose 110 + CT no hemorrhage + no bleeding risks → which treatment?
ask: Which of the following is most likely to improve his functional outcome?

whyNot.D: No benefit in acute stroke and adds **bleeding risk**
whyNot.E: Prevents later events; does **not dissolve** the clot

why: **Acute ischemic stroke within 4.5 hours, no hemorrhage on CT, no contraindication** = IV thrombolysis. **Alteplase** converts plasminogen to plasmin, lysing the embolus and reopening the artery.

drug.name: Alteplase
drug.how: Converts plasminogen to plasmin, lysing fibrin
drug.use: Ischemic stroke within 3-4.5 h, STEMI, massive PE
drug.watch: Hemorrhage (intracranial); excluded by recent bleeding, surgery, stroke, high BP

stem: A 27-year-old woman has had 3 days of sneezing, watery nasal discharge, itchy eyes and nasal congestion every spring when the grass pollen count is high. She asks for a short-term remedy to relieve her stuffy nose before a long flight. She has no hypertension or cardiac disease.
oneliner: 27F + seasonal sneezing, watery rhinorrhea, itchy eyes + nasal congestion + wants short-term relief of stuffiness → which drug?
ask: Which of the following drugs would most effectively relieve her nasal congestion?

whyNot.A: **Prazosin**: an alpha-1 blocker; dilates mucosal vessels and can **worsen** congestion
whyNot.B: **Albuterol**: β2 agonist for bronchospasm; does not shrink nasal mucosa
whyNot.D: **Isoproterenol**: nonselective β agonist; vasodilates, no decongestion
whyNot.E: **Atropine**: dries secretions but does not shrink swollen mucosa

why: **Allergic rhinitis with congestion** from dilated mucosal vessels responds to an **α1 agonist** (phenylephrine, pseudoephedrine), which **constricts mucosal vessels** and reduces swelling.

drug.name: Phenylephrine
drug.how: Stimulates α1 receptors, constricting mucosal and systemic arterioles
drug.use: Nasal decongestion, hypotension, mydriasis, supraventricular tachycardia (reflex)
drug.watch: Hypertension, reflex bradycardia, rebound congestion with topical overuse

stem: A 14-year-old girl with familial dysautonomia has dizziness and near-fainting on standing. Her blood pressure falls from 108/68 mm Hg supine to 72/40 mm Hg standing without a rise in heart rate. Compression stockings and fludrocortisone have not helped. Her physician adds an oral drug that raises vascular tone directly.
oneliner: 14F + familial dysautonomia + orthostasis, BP 108/68 → 72/40 without tachycardia + failed fludrocortisone and stockings → add which oral drug?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate drug to add?

whyNot.A: **Isoproterenol**: β agonist; vasodilates and lowers pressure further
whyNot.B: **Propranolol**: β blocker; no pressor effect and may worsen orthostasis
whyNot.C: **Bethanechol**: muscarinic agonist for urinary retention; not a vasoconstrictor

why: **Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension refractory to volume expanders** is treated with a pure **α1 agonist vasoconstrictor**, **midodrine**, which raises vascular tone without autonomic reflexes.

drug.name: Midodrine
drug.how: Active metabolite stimulates α1 receptors, constricting arterioles and veins
drug.watch: Supine hypertension, piloerection, urinary retention, reflex bradycardia

stem: A 62-year-old man with known coronary artery disease has new crushing chest pressure at rest that has lasted 10 minutes. He has taken no medication yet. Blood pressure is 142/86 mm Hg and heart rate 96/min. He takes no erectile dysfunction drugs.
oneliner: 62M + known CAD + new crushing chest pressure at rest x 10 min + BP 142/86, no ED drugs → fastest pain relief?
ask: Which drug gives the fastest relief of his chest pain?

whyNot.A: **Beta-blocker**: lowers heart rate and oxygen demand over time, but is not the quickest relief of an attack
whyNot.B: **Antiplatelet**: limits clot growth, but does not relieve ischemic pain
whyNot.D: **Calcium channel blocker**: slow onset, used for prevention, not rescue
whyNot.E: **Late sodium current blocker**: chronic add-on for angina, not for an acute attack

why: **Ischemic chest pain at rest that needs relief now** = sublingual **nitroglycerin**, which dilates veins within minutes and cuts preload and oxygen demand.

drug.name: Nitroglycerin
drug.how: Releases nitric oxide, raises cGMP, relaxes vascular smooth muscle (mainly veins) and lowers preload
drug.use: Acute angina (sublingual), chronic angina, acute heart failure
drug.watch: Headache, flushing, hypotension; never with PDE-5 inhibitors; tolerance

stem: A 60-year-old man had an anterior myocardial infarction 3 months ago. For 6 weeks he has had low mood, loss of interest, poor sleep, guilt and poor concentration. He denies thoughts of self-harm. His cardiac status is stable.
oneliner: 60M + anterior MI 3 mo ago + 6 wk low mood, anhedonia, guilt, poor sleep + stable heart → best drug for his mood?
ask: Which drug is the best choice to treat his depression?

whyNot.A: **Tricyclic**: slows cardiac conduction and causes arrhythmias; avoid after MI
whyNot.B: **Benzodiazepine**: treats anxiety, not the core symptoms of depression
whyNot.C: **MAO inhibitor**: hypertensive crisis with tyramine and many interactions; not first line

why: **Low mood and loss of interest for over 2 weeks after an MI** = major depression, which itself raises later mortality. An **SSRI such as sertraline** is the cardiac-safe choice.

drug.name: Sertraline
drug.how: Blocks serotonin reuptake, raising synaptic serotonin
drug.use: Depression, anxiety disorders, OCD, PTSD, panic disorder
drug.watch: GI upset, sexual dysfunction, serotonin syndrome, hyponatremia, bleeding risk with antiplatelets

stem: A 48-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and microalbuminuria has had a dry, tickling cough for 2 months. It began a few weeks after lisinopril was started for his blood pressure. He does not smoke, lung examination is clear, and a chest x-ray is normal. His blood pressure is now well controlled and the urine albumin has fallen, so the team wants to keep this kind of kidney protection.
oneliner: 48M + diabetes with microalbuminuria + dry cough 2 mo after lisinopril + normal chest x-ray + BP controlled → switch to?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate replacement?

whyNot.A: Same class as lisinopril: **ACE inhibitors share the cough**
whyNot.C: **Direct vasodilator**: lowers BP but gives no kidney protection and causes reflex tachycardia
whyNot.D: **Central alpha-2 agonist**: lowers BP, no kidney protection, rebound hypertension
whyNot.E: **Beta-blocker**: no protection of the glomerulus and masks hypoglycemia in diabetes

why: **ACE inhibitor cough** comes from **bradykinin buildup**. An **ARB such as losartan** blocks the **AT1 receptor** without stopping bradykinin breakdown, so it keeps the kidney benefit and spares the cough.

drug.name: Losartan
drug.how: Blocks AT1 receptors; ACE is untouched, so bradykinin does not rise
drug.use: Hypertension, diabetic nephropathy, heart failure; replaces an ACE inhibitor that caused cough
drug.watch: Hyperkalemia, acute kidney injury in bilateral renal artery stenosis, teratogenic; cough and angioedema far less common than with ACE inhibitors

idea.rule: ACE inhibitor cough is a bradykinin effect, so switch to an ARB, which leaves bradykinin alone.
also: ACE inhibitors also cause angioedema through bradykinin
Both classes cause hyperkalemia and are teratogenic
Both lower efferent arteriolar tone and protect the diabetic kidney
Sacubitril (neprilysin inhibitor) is paired with valsartan, not an ACE inhibitor, to avoid angioedema

stem: A 38-year-old woman has episodes of pounding headache, sweating and palpitations lasting minutes. Today her blood pressure is 210/120 mm Hg and pulse is 118/min. Plasma metanephrines are markedly high and CT shows a 4-cm right adrenal mass. Surgery is planned, and the team must start medication for the days before it.
oneliner: 38F + episodic headache, sweating, palpitations + BP 210/120 + high metanephrines + adrenal mass + surgery planned → which drug first?
ask: Which of the following should be started first?

whyNot.A: A **beta-blocker alone** leaves alpha-1 vasoconstriction unopposed and can worsen hypertension
whyNot.C: Same problem as propranolol: **beta-1 selective** blockade still does not stop alpha-1 vasoconstriction
whyNot.D: **Thiazide**: volume depletion with no control of catecholamine-driven vasoconstriction
whyNot.E: **Short beta-blocker** is added only after alpha blockade, mainly for tachycardia

why: **Paroxysmal hypertension + high metanephrines + adrenal mass** = **pheochromocytoma**. Give an **alpha blocker first (phenoxybenzamine)**; a beta-blocker alone leaves **alpha-1 vasoconstriction unopposed** and can cause a hypertensive crisis. A beta-blocker is added later for tachycardia.

drug.name: Phenoxybenzamine
drug.how: Covalently blocks alpha-1 and alpha-2 receptors, so catecholamine surges cannot cause vasoconstriction
drug.use: Pheochromocytoma before surgery (phentolamine, a reversible alpha blocker, is used for acute crises)
drug.watch: Orthostatic hypotension, reflex tachycardia, nasal congestion, inhibited ejaculation

idea.rule: In catecholamine excess, block alpha first and add a beta-blocker second.
also: Cocaine intoxication: avoid beta-blockers alone; benzodiazepines and phentolamine first
Clonidine withdrawal: restore clonidine or give phentolamine, not a beta-blocker alone
Phentolamine is the reversible alpha blocker for acute crises

stem: A 38-year-old Black man is found to have blood pressure of 158/98 mm Hg on repeated visits. He has no diabetes, kidney disease, proteinuria or heart failure, and his serum potassium and creatinine are normal. He is about to start his first antihypertensive.
oneliner: 38M Black + BP 158/98 on repeated visits + no diabetes, kidney disease or heart failure → best first drug?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial drug?

whyNot.A: **ACE inhibitors** lower BP less in Black patients without kidney disease or heart failure, and carry higher angioedema risk
whyNot.C: **ARBs** share the weaker response with ACE inhibitors in this group
whyNot.D: **Beta-blockers** are not first-line for uncomplicated hypertension; he has no angina or prior MI
whyNot.E: **Central alpha-2 agonist**: a later add-on, with rebound hypertension on stopping

answer: A thiazide-type diuretic (or a calcium channel blocker)
why: In **Black patients with uncomplicated hypertension**, a **thiazide-type diuretic or calcium channel blocker** gives the larger fall in pressure; renin-angiotensin blockers work best when there is **proteinuria, diabetic nephropathy or heart failure**, none of which he has.

drug.name: Chlorthalidone
drug.how: Blocks the Na+/Cl- cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule, causing natriuresis and later lowered vascular resistance
drug.use: Primary hypertension (especially in Black patients), edema, calcium kidney stones
drug.watch: Hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hyperuricemia and gout, hyperglycemia, hypercalcemia

idea.rule: Low-renin hypertension (common in Black and older patients) responds best to thiazides and calcium channel blockers.
also: Amlodipine is an equal first choice
Older adults, often low-renin, respond well to thiazides and CCBs
Primary hyperaldosteronism (renin suppressed) responds to spironolactone
Proteinuric CKD shifts the choice to an ACE inhibitor or ARB in any patient
